newsitem.title: ALBANIA: FEATURE - Violence dashes hopes for tourism boom in Albania.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Violence dashes hopes for tourism boom in Albania.

text.p: Hopes that tourism development along Albania's picturesque Adriatic coast would bring greater prosperity to Europe's poorest nation have been dashed by the violence that has gripped the country for months.

Tour operators, hoteliers and restaurateurs in this southern Albanian town say their budding industry may have been dealt a fatal blow by the unrest sparked by the collapse of dubious investment funds earlier this year.

"We had people like the Gettys and the Rothschilds visit our area," tour operator Auron Tare told Reuters. "I heard that Prince Charles was also interested in coming this summer. I think he may have to change his plans."
Before the violence erupted, some 80,000 foreigners were visiting Albania every year, up from 20,000 a year under communist rule which crumbled in late 1990.
But most of the travellers were on business and officials estimate a mere 2,000 tourists visited Albania last year.
Now even that number looks unattainable.

More than 1,500 people have been killed since March, when the south of the country slid into anarchy after five local pyramid investment schemes folded, leaving hundreds of thousands of people destitute.
Mobs raided state buildings and army arsenals, looting weapons which have ended up in the hands of gangs or been distributed among the region's youth.

The West has sent a 7,000-strong multi-national force to protect desperately needed foreign aid and also help keep order during a snap general election on Sunday which is seen as Albania's last hope to restore peace and order.
IMPRESSION OF VIOLENCE AND DANGER
"Even if peace returns after this election, it will take years to erase the impression of violence and danger associated with Albania," Tare said.
Taking advantage of booming tourism on the nearby Greek island of Corfu, Tare and his Australian girlfriend began their business by bringing visitors over for day trips.
"We started in 1991 with two old English ladies and we expanded to chartering our own boat," he said.

They turned a decrepit 1930s Italian villa overlooking the harbour into a guest house, began organising tours to the nearby ancient site of Butrint and offered trekking trips. That attracted many jet-setters who owned houses in Corfu, he said.
Even during 50 years of Stalinist isolation, Sarande retained some of its old-world charm, despite a cluster of communist-built apartment buildings north of the harbour.
But while lawlessness rules, Sarande's trademark palm trees are being chopped down to make way for a splurge of concrete buildings.
"They are rushing to build now that there is no state authority to stop them from taking over any land they like," said 60-year-old Hujredin Cakeri, sitting at his family's coffee shop.

He said that, instead of investing in pyramids, his sons put all their money in the cafe in 1993, hoping tourism would offer a better return. With the number of hotel beds in Albania estimated at only 9,000, their project seemed profitable.
"In the beginning we had lots of Greeks and Italians, some on day trips and others who spent their holidays here. Now it's empty, nobody comes," he said.
GUNFIRE AND EXPLOSIONS ROUTINE
Waiters at the numerous seaside cafes and restaurants are no longer startled by the sound of gunfire and explosions.
Their brand-new buildings testify to the eagerness of international organisations to help Albania find a way out of its poverty, primarily by funding small-scale developments.
Venjel Shtuka borrowed the equivalent of $55,000 from the European Union's PHARE programme to build one of the town's few hotels.
"I finished it in July 1996 and I operated until the troubles in March. Now there is no business and I can't even make my loan payments," he said.
